speaker: Lisa Blatt
title: Arguing In Front of SCOTUS | Interview: Lisa Blatt
question: At the U.S. Supreme Court, how do justices actually decide cases in practice compared to rigid judicial philosophies like originalism or textualism?
guest: They have no choice with some stuff. I think they try their best. Obviously, they look at the text because why wouldn't you? But I don't call that textualism. There's a piece of paper telling you how to apply the law, so yeah, you're going to start there. I think it depends on the case—whether we're talking a business case, a constitutional law case, or a case about race. So I break it down to what type of case it is, and whether it's going to be driven by ideology, the facts of the case, the law more generally, or how the law is developing in this area. It just depends on the case. I think about the law in terms of an advocate. My only job is to try to win a case for a client. You just have to get to five and win; if you can get to nine, great. I started doing this under Chief Justice Rehnquist—none of them are the same except Thomas—and my approach to law hasn't changed even though the Court has entirely turned over.

points.core: Justices start with statutory text out of practical necessity rather than rigid textualism.

points.core: The decisive driver shifts across subject-matter categories rather than following one method.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
In practice, justices decide cases through a mix of methods rather than by mechanically applying a single philosophy. Even self-described originalists and textualists routinely weigh precedent, practical consequences, institutional concerns, and their own sense of how the law should work. Justice Scalia called himself a "faint-hearted" originalist, and current justices who share the label often disagree with each other about what the text or history requires, which shows the methods leave considerable room for judgment.

Political scientists find that ideology predicts votes well in the contested, high-profile cases: the "attitudinal model" holds that justices' policy preferences drive outcomes, with legal reasoning supplying the justification. Critics point to selective use of history, or to textualism giving way to doctrines like "major questions" when the text points to an unwelcome result.

That picture is incomplete, though. Roughly 40 to 50 percent of cases are typically unanimous, many splits don't follow ideological lines, and justices sometimes vote against their apparent preferences (Gorsuch in Bostock and McGirt, for example). Strategic bargaining to hold a majority, and concern for the Court's legitimacy, also shape opinions.

So philosophy constrains and guides, but judgment, values, and pragmatism fill the gaps.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In practice, U.S. Supreme Court justices rarely apply originalism, textualism, or any single philosophy as a mechanical formula; instead, decision-making is pluralistic, collegial, and pragmatic. Even self-described originalists and textualists routinely weigh precedent, structural principles, longstanding historical practice, and real-world consequences alongside constitutional or statutory text. Because five votes are required to form a majority, adjudication is also strategic: justices bargain over language, narrow holdings, and adopt incremental compromises to hold a coalition together.

Empirical legal scholarship further shows that ideological priors and personal judgment heavily shape outcomes because cases reaching the Court usually involve ambiguous text and contested history—which explains why two committed textualists or originalists often reach opposite conclusions in the same dispute. Institutional considerations, such as preserving public legitimacy, crafting workable rules for lower courts, and avoiding disruptive social or economic fallout, likewise temper methodological purity. Formal philosophies still matter, especially as textualism and originalism increasingly set the terms of argument, but they function less as deterministic algorithms and more as disciplining frameworks within which justices debate and justify their rulings.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
In practice, justices decide cases more pragmatically than any single philosophy would suggest. After oral argument, they meet privately in conference, cast tentative votes, and the senior justice in the majority assigns the opinion. Drafts then circulate, and votes and reasoning can change as justices bargain over wording to hold a majority. Precedent, stare decisis, the facts of the case, practical consequences, institutional legitimacy, and the narrowness of the question all shape outcomes.

Originalism and textualism matter, but they work more like toolkits than algorithms. Justices who share a method often disagree on the result. In *Bostock* (2020), for example, Gorsuch and Alito both used textualism and reached opposite conclusions. Even self-described originalists set aside history when precedent or practicality weighs heavily. Political scientists debate how much ideology drives votes ("attitudinal model") versus legal reasoning or strategic coalition-building, and the evidence suggests all three play a role, especially in contested cases. Still, roughly 40–50% of decisions are unanimous most terms, which shows that ordinary legal reasoning settles many cases. Ideological splits mainly appear in the high-profile minority of cases.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
In practice, Supreme Court justices rarely apply a single judicial philosophy like originalism or textualism with mechanical rigidity. Instead, most operate as methodological pluralists, blending text, history, precedent, constitutional structure, and practical consequences depending on the case. Even staunch originalists routinely defer to established precedent (*stare decisis*) to preserve legal stability, while pragmatists still anchor their rulings in statutory text when it is clear.

Deciding cases is also a deeply institutional and collaborative process. Because a majority requires five votes, justices frequently negotiate, narrow their reasoning, or adopt incremental holdings to build and hold coalitions. Beyond doctrine, empirical scholarship shows that justices’ broader ideological commitments, professional backgrounds, and institutional concerns—such as protecting the Court’s legitimacy and crafting workable rules for lower courts—quietly shape which interpretive tools they prioritize when text and history are ambiguous. Rather than rigid algorithms that dictate outcomes, philosophies like originalism and textualism function more as guiding frameworks and shared vocabularies through which justices justify and debate contested legal judgments.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Supreme Court justices use philosophies like originalism and textualism to guide how they interpret legal texts. In practice, they also have to decide which precedents control, which facts matter, and how broadly to rule. Justices who share a philosophy can still disagree about how it applies. In *Bostock v. Clayton County*, for example, the majority and dissenters all appealed to the statutory text but disagreed over whether Title VII’s ban on sex discrimination covered firing someone for being gay or transgender.

After oral argument, the justices discuss the case and take an initial vote in private. As draft opinions circulate, they can request changes, join a narrower opinion, write separately, or change their votes. The published ruling reflects the reasoning that could command a majority, when there is one. Judicial philosophy shapes that reasoning alongside precedent, judgment about the case, and the need to build agreement.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Supreme Court justices use originalism and textualism to guide their reasoning, but neither method dictates a vote in every case. Originalism asks what a constitutional provision meant when it was adopted. Textualism focuses on the meaning of the enacted words. Two justices who share a method can still disagree about which historical evidence matters, how to read a phrase in context, or whether precedent controls.

In practice, justices weigh the text, precedent, history, and the facts before them. They differ in how much weight they give each, and some also consider how a ruling would work in practice. Their values and ideological commitments can influence those judgments, especially when the legal sources point in different directions. After oral argument, the justices cast preliminary votes in private conference. As draft opinions circulate, a justice may change position or join a narrower opinion, so the Court’s ultimate reasoning can reflect what a majority is willing to endorse together.
